title: Cell Counting Using a Hemocytometer

references.label: General microbiology/molecular biology laboratory manuals (ASM curriculum resources)

purpose: To manually determine the concentration of cells in a suspension, commonly for seeding cultures at a defined density or reporting culture growth.
principle: A hemocytometer's etched grid sits a precisely known distance beneath the coverslip, defining a chamber of known volume over each counting square; counting cells within a defined set of squares using a consistent boundary rule, and applying the chamber's known volume together with any dilution factor used, yields the concentration of the original suspension.
requiredMaterials: Hemocytometer and coverslip, cleaned before use
requiredReagents: Trypan blue (if a combined count/viability assessment is desired)

procedure.instruction: Mix the cell suspension thoroughly to ensure an even distribution before sampling.
If assessing viability, mix an aliquot with trypan blue at the method-specified ratio and note this dilution factor.
Mount the coverslip on the hemocytometer, confirming correct seating (visible Newton's rings).
Load a small volume into the loading channel by capillary action, avoiding overfilling.
Under the microscope, count cells in a defined set of grid squares (commonly the four large corner squares), applying a consistent boundary-cell counting rule.
Calculate the concentration using the hemocytometer's known chamber volume and any dilution factor applied.

observations: A cell density within the hemocytometer's practical counting range (neither too sparse nor too crowded to count reliably) in each counted square.
interpretation: The calculated concentration reflects the cell density of the original suspension; if paired with trypan blue, live (dye-excluding) and dead (dye-included) cells can be separately tallied to also report viability percentage.
criticalNotes: Apply the same boundary-cell counting rule (which edges' touching cells are included) consistently across all counted squares to avoid systematic bias.
Recount if squares show excessive cell density or clumping, diluting the sample further if needed.
precautions: Handle any biological sample per its risk assessment.
Clean the hemocytometer and coverslip immediately after use to prevent dried residue affecting future counts.
limitations: Manual counting is subject to operator variability, and counting too few total cells increases statistical uncertainty in the resulting concentration estimate.
Clumped or unevenly distributed cells reduce counting accuracy regardless of technique.
